svg.title: Five counter-intuitive truths about Layer 3 design, each with the mechanism behind it
svg.desc: Five rows. Truth 1: a BGP policy can be overridden by an IGP metric, because criteria one to seven can all tie and criterion eight, the IGP metric to the next hop, then decides. Truth 2: protocol choice is an operating model question, team familiarity weighs most and theoretical scalability weighs least. Truth 3: summarization hides information, a failed /24 stays hidden behind a living summary and traffic is dropped inside the area. Truth 4: faster convergence is not automatically better, a 50 ms BFD timer with no throttling lets a 200 ms flap trigger a network-wide SPF run. Truth 5: each extra protocol multiplies complexity, two protocols mean two redistribution directions and three protocols mean six. A note at the bottom says a design that cannot be explained on a whiteboard in five minutes will not be operable at three in the morning.
svg.text: Five things that are true about Layer 3 design, and are not what the configuration guide implies
Each row is a mechanism, not an opinion — the mechanism is what makes it worth a chapter
THE TRUTH
WHY IT IS TRUE, MECHANICALLY
WHAT IT CHANGES IN THE DESIGN
A BGP policy you designed can be
undone by an IGP metric
Criteria 1–7 (Weight, LP, local origin, AS_PATH, Origin, MED) can all tie.
Criterion 8 — the IGP metric to NEXT_HOP — then decides, and that
metric came from a bandwidth formula nobody chose.
Design the IGP cost and the BGP attributes
together. Change one, check the other.
“show ip bgp” changing is not the FIB changing.
Choosing a protocol is an operating-
model question, not a technical one
Real weight order: what the team can troubleshoot → multivendor need
→ path-control need → convergence → theoretical scalability (lowest).
The design document must state why this
protocol, and the reason must include the
team, not only the standard.
Summarization hides information;
the price is losing visibility
One /24 fails. The summary 10.1.0.0/16 survives as long as any other
/24 is reachable. Traffic keeps entering the area and dies inside it.
Pair every summary with a null0 route.
A summary without null0 is a design flaw.
Troubleshoot inside the area, not at the core.
Faster convergence is not
always better
BFD at 50 ms, Hello at 1 s, no SPF throttling: a 200 ms optic flap
runs SPF across the whole area, the CPU saturates, and rehashing moves
TCP flows — reordering, retransmits, collapsed throughput.
Tiered response: detect in ms, repair
locally in 100 ms, recompute SPF in
seconds. Throttling is a requirement.
Each extra protocol doubles the
complexity; it does not add one
1 protocol = 1 path set. 2 = 2 redistribution directions. 3 = 6
directions, and the B↔C pair usually appears by accident, not by design.
Keep the protocol count small. Dual-
point dual-direction redistribution costs
more than the problem it solves.
The through-line: every truth above is a case where the network obeys a mechanism the designer never chose on purpose.
If a design cannot be explained on a whiteboard in five minutes, it will not be operable at 3 a.m. when it is broken.
